title: The blind men and the elephant
hook: each man touches one part of the elephant and quarrels with the rest (Udana 6.4)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Stoicism, a neighbor to this path, with a similar calm and different reasons. Your line: same calm, different reasons.

Year two began with an elephant's footprint. Right view ends with the whole elephant. In the city of Savatthi, the monks come back from their alms round shaken. All over town, teachers and their followers are arguing about the big questions: is the world eternal, is the soul the body. Each side says only this is true, everything else is foolish. The arguing has turned into shouting, and the shouting into wounding words. The monks tell the Buddha. He doesn't declare a winner. He tells them about a king who once borrowed an elephant.
screen: `MONKS COME BACK SHAKEN.` → `ONLY THIS IS TRUE.` → `A KING BORROWS AN ELEPHANT.`

segments.voice: The story is in the Udana, a short book of inspired sayings, chapter six. Long ago, the Buddha says, a king of Savatthi had his servant gather every man in the city who had been born blind. Then he had an elephant brought, and let each man touch one part: the head, the ear, the tusk, the trunk, the body, the foot, the back, the tail, the tuft at the end of the tail. Then the king asked: what is an elephant like? Those who touched the head said: like a water pot. The ear: a winnowing basket. The tusk: a plowshare. The trunk: a plow pole. The body: a storehouse. The foot: a post. The back: a mortar. The tail: a pestle. The tuft: a broom. And then, the text says, they began to argue, each insisting the elephant is like this, not like that, until they came to blows. And the king was delighted. The quarreling teachers are like this, the Buddha says: they don't see the whole, and so they fight over the part. The story is aimed at anyone, of any group, who seizes a part and calls it the whole, including his own monks. The big questions in the background are the same ones Malunkyaputta wanted answered, the ones left aside in the arrow story. This story has neighbors: Jains, Hindus and Sufi poets like Rumi tell their own versions, each with its own lesson. In the Udana, the lesson closes the section on right view: each holds a part.
screen: `A KING GATHERS THE BLIND.` · `A POT, A BASKET, A BROOM.` · `THEY COME TO BLOWS.` · `SEIZING A PART AS THE WHOLE.` · then, large: `EACH HOLDS A PART.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a view held by someone you disagree with, not to adopt it, just to touch it, and ask: what part of the elephant might they be holding, and what did they touch that I didn't? If irritation comes, notice it, and come back to the breath. Let both your part and theirs be parts.
Jaccandha, born blind. Each touches one part of the elephant and fights over the whole: the Buddha's picture of clinging to partial views.
Your line: each holds a part. No single hand covers the whole elephant. That's day three hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers tell the story of the blind men and the elephant to warn against clinging to partial views and quarreling over them, and it is widely told in other traditions too.

fork.setup: you're the king. you've shown each blind man one part of the elephant, and now they're fighting about what an elephant is like. what does the king do, in the story?
options: he stops the fight and explains the whole elephant.
fork.reveal: the text says the king was delighted; the Buddha uses the scene to show how people who see only one side wrangle.

what a scholar hears: Udana 6.4 (Tittha Sutta) is set against wanderers quarreling over the ten undeclared points; Jain, Hindu and Sufi versions (Rumi's Masnavi has an elephant in a dark room) draw their own morals.

an arrow, the Buddha's image for pain

chat.says: Why do people with different views fight so hard over who's right?
options: Like the blind men, each touches one part and takes it for the whole.
Because only one group ever holds the truth, and the rest are fools.
Because arguing loudly is the surest way to reach the whole truth.
chat.meaning: In the Udana, blind men each touch one part of the elephant and fight; the Buddha says quarreling teachers seize a part as the whole.

Malunkyaputta.meaning: the monk who demanded answers to the big questions
